summary: Defines a fully specified forward error correction scheme using Reed-Solomon codes, applied to reliable delivery of data over channels where packets either arrive intact or are lost. Extra repair packets let receivers rebuild lost data.

eli5.summary: If a puzzle has a few pieces missing, spare pieces cut with a clever rule can fill the gaps. This note describes such spare pieces so a file can be rebuilt even when some packets get lost.

questions: how does forward error correction recover lost packets
how does reed-solomon erasure coding recover lost packets
subtitle: Reed-Solomon erasure codes that let receivers rebuild a file from any k of the packets that arrive.

tldr.problem: When data is sent to many receivers over a channel that drops packets, receivers need a way to recover lost data without asking for retransmission.
tldr.mechanism: The sender splits an object into source blocks of k source symbols and adds repair symbols computed with Reed-Solomon codes over GF(2^m). Any k of the encoding symbols of a block are enough to recover the k source symbols.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines FEC Encoding IDs 2 and 5 and FEC Instance ID 0 under Encoding ID 129, all compatible with Luigi Rizzo's Reed-Solomon codec. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Recovery rule
facts.value: Any k encoding symbols give the k source symbols

today: RFC 5510 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The sections above are therefore still the specification of these Reed-Solomon FEC schemes.

sections.title: Why Reed-Solomon FEC
sections.content:
Forward Error Correction (FEC) is a classical way to make multicast and broadcast transmissions more reliable. The framework for using FEC in content delivery protocols is in RFC 5052, and RFC 3453 describes applications of FEC for content delivery.

Newer schemes such as RFC 5053 and RFC 5170 use sparse graphs and matrices. They are efficient to process but not optimal at correcting losses when objects are small. The schemes in this RFC belong to the class of Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) codes, which are optimal in that sense: a receiver can recover the k source symbols from any set of exactly k encoding symbols.

The codes are also systematic, so the k source symbols are themselves part of the encoding symbols. The goal is to specify an implementation compatible with the Reed-Solomon codec of Luigi Rizzo, which many applications already use.
sections.eli5: If you send a friend a jigsaw puzzle by post and some pieces get lost, they cannot finish it. Here you also send a few spare pieces made by a special rule, so any lost pieces can be worked out again.

sections.title: Symbols, Blocks and the Erasure Channel
sections.content:
The RFC works on a packet erasure channel: a path where each packet is either received without corruption or dropped, for example by a congested router. The location of erased symbols MUST be known.

An object of L bytes is cut into N source blocks. Each block holds k source symbols of E bytes. The encoder produces n encoding symbols for the block, made of the k source symbols plus n_r repair symbols, so n = k + n_r. The code rate is k/n.

Several symbols can travel in one packet. G is the number of encoding symbols per group, and a group's relationship to the source block is derived from a single Encoding Symbol ID.
sections.eli5: The file is cut into batches of pieces. For each batch you add some extra pieces, and the share of real pieces in the batch is the code rate.

sections.title: FEC Payload ID and Encoding ID 2
sections.content:
FEC Encoding ID 2 uses Reed-Solomon codes over GF(2^m), with m between 2 and 16. Every source or repair packet carries exactly one FEC Payload ID made of two fields, and their sizes depend on m.

  • The Source Block Number is 32-m bits long and gives at most 2^(32-m) blocks per object.
  • The Encoding Symbol ID is m bits long and gives at most 2^m encoding symbols per block. Values 0 to k-1 are source symbols and the remaining n-k values are repair symbols.

When a packet holds several symbols, the Payload ID names the first one and the others follow by incrementing the ID. The default is m = 8 and G = 1, and a decoder that is told nothing MUST assume those values.

The object transmission information (FEC OTI) carries the transfer length L, symbol length E, maximum block length B, max_n, and the scheme-specific m and G. It can be sent in an EXT_FTI header extension (for example in ALC or NORM) or in the FDT Instance of a FLUTE session, where m and G are Base64 encoded. The RFC does not say when to use which format.
sections.eli5: Every packet has a small label saying which batch it belongs to and which piece of the batch it is, so the receiver can put it in the right place.

sections.title: Encoding ID 5 and Instance ID 0
sections.content:
FEC Encoding ID 5 is the special case of GF(2^8) with no encoding symbol group, so m = 8 and G = 1 and exactly one symbol per packet. Its Payload ID is a 24-bit Source Block Number followed by an 8-bit Encoding Symbol ID. It defines no scheme-specific OTI elements.

For the Under-Specified Small Block Systematic FEC Scheme (FEC Encoding ID 129) from RFC 5445, this RFC assigns FEC Instance ID 0 to Reed-Solomon codes over GF(2^8) with no encoding symbol group. It uses the formats of RFC 5445, and MAY use the block partitioning of RFC 5052 or another algorithm. For example, a sender could change block length dynamically to match the loss rate seen by NORM receivers.
sections.eli5: There is a plain, fixed version for the most common setup, with one piece per packet, so nobody has to choose any settings.

sections.title: Choosing Block and Symbol Counts
sections.content:
For Encoding IDs 2 and 5, the block partitioning algorithm of RFC 5052 MUST be used. The field size limits a block to q-1 = 2^m - 1 encoding symbols, which is 255 when m = 8.

The sender computes max1_B = floor((2^m - 1) * CR) from the target code rate CR, and a codec MAY add its own limit max2_B. Then B = min(max1_B, max2_B). Only the coder needs this, because B is sent to the decoder in the OTI.

The recommended n-algorithm is max_n = ceil(B / CR), an error ("invalid code rate") if max_n exceeds 2^m - 1, and n = floor(k * max_n / B). A receiver can use the same formula for n to estimate memory needs, but it MUST be ready for symbols with an ID at or above the computed n.
sections.eli5: Before sending, you work out how many spare pieces each batch gets, based on how much protection you want, and you tell the receivers the limits.

sections.title: How the Reed-Solomon Code Works
sections.content:
An [n,k] Reed-Solomon code is a linear block code that turns k elements of a finite field GF(q) into n elements, with n at most q-1. Here q = 2^m. Field elements are binary polynomials, and the RFC fixes one irreducible primitive polynomial for each m from 2 to 16. For m = 8 it is 1+x^2+x^3+x^4+x^8.

Encoding is e = s * GM, where s is the source vector and GM a generator matrix of k rows and n columns. GM starts from a Vandermonde matrix V built from powers of alpha, a root of the chosen polynomial. To make the code systematic, the first k columns of V are inverted and multiplied by V, giving GM = (V_{k,k}^-1) * V_{k,n}. The first k columns are then the identity matrix, so the source symbols appear unchanged.

Decoding takes the k columns of GM for the symbols that arrived. That k*k submatrix is always invertible, so inverting it and multiplying the received vector recovers the source. Classical Gauss-Jordan inversion costs O(k^3) operations and the multiplication O(k^2).

For packets, each symbol is S m-bit elements. The u-th elements of all source symbols form the u-th source vector, so every position uses the same erasure pattern and the matrix inversion is done only once.

Repair symbols can be produced on demand: to make symbol e_j with k <= j < n, multiply the source vectors by column j of GM. A sender can start with few repair symbols and make more if losses are observed. Short last symbols are virtually padded with zero elements, and the padding need not be sent.
sections.eli5: The spare pieces are made by mixing the real pieces together with a fixed maths recipe. Any group of pieces as big as the original batch is enough to solve the recipe backwards and get the real ones back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC covers only the extra threats a content delivery protocol faces when it uses this FEC building block. Attacks can target confidentiality, object integrity, or the receiver's behaviour, for example by making decoding expensive, and can hit either the data flow or the FEC parameters.

For confidentiality, encrypt the whole object before FEC encoding or encrypt per packet, for example with IPsec ESP; this is RECOMMENDED if access control matters, and is not made easier or harder by FEC. For integrity, it lists object-level digital signatures, per-packet signatures, a group MAC such as HMAC-SHA-256, and TESLA. A group MAC cannot stop one member forging packets, and TESLA needs a small delay of a second or more to check a packet. If corruption is a concern, at least one of these SHOULD be used.

Altering the FEC OTI breaks decoding: changing B changes the block partitioning, and setting m to 16 instead of 8 with Encoding ID 2 adds load and breaks decoding. OTI integrity is therefore RECOMMENDED, using per-packet protection for EXT_FTI, an XML signature for an FDT Instance, and a signature on a session description for out-of-band OTI.
sections.eli5: Someone could slip fake pieces into the pile or change the instructions, so the sender should sign the pieces and the instructions to let receivers trust them.

fields.name: Source Block Number
fields.desc: Which source block of the object the symbol comes from.

fields.name: Encoding Symbol ID
fields.desc: Which encoding symbol of the block the packet carries.

fields.name: Transfer Length (L), high part
fields.desc: Object length in bytes; the field spans the next word as well.

fields.name: Encoding Symbol Length (E)
fields.desc: Length of each encoding symbol in bytes.

fields.name: MaxBlkLen (B)
fields.desc: Maximum number of source symbols in a block.

fields.name: max_n
fields.desc: Maximum number of encoding symbols for any block.

items.title: Encoding ID 2
items.text: Reed-Solomon over GF(2^m), m from 2 to 16, with optional symbol groups.

items.title: Encoding ID 5
items.text: Reed-Solomon over GF(2^8), one symbol per packet.

items.title: Instance ID 0
items.text: Reed-Solomon over GF(2^8) under Small Block Systematic Encoding ID 129.
